# Defaults That Use Other Variables

A variable's `default` can be built from other variables, such as `default: "{{ .ProjectName }}-state"`. Runbooks fills in the real value when it renders, using whatever the other fields hold at that moment.

The form never shows the `{{ }}` syntax. A linked default appears as a token for each variable it uses, named the way that variable's field is labelled. A default that does more than insert a variable (a conditional or a function) appears as one token that says what it's based on.

- **Hover** over a linked value to see its expression.
- **Click** it to edit the expression.
- **Click the X** to clear it and type your own value.

## In an Inputs block

`ServiceName` defaults to the app name with a `-service` suffix. Change `AppName` and watch the preview below follow it.

<Inputs id="naming">
```yaml
variables:
  - name: AppName
    type: string
    description: Name of the application
    default: web
  - name: ServiceName
    type: string
    description: Defaults to the app name with a "-service" suffix
    default: "{{ .AppName }}-service"
```
</Inputs>

<TemplateInline id="naming-preview" inputsId="naming" outputPath="service.txt">
```txt
Service name: {{ .inputs.ServiceName }}
```
</TemplateInline>

## In a Template

This template's `boilerplate.yml` has linked defaults of every kind:

- `BucketName` is the project name plus `-state`.
- `ReplicaBucket` is the same as `BucketName`.
- `InstanceSize` depends on `Environment`.
- `CatalogRepositories` has an entry built from the project name.
- `DefaultTags` has a key and a value built from other variables.

Generate it, then change `ProjectName` or `Environment` and look at `settings.yml`.

<Template id="linked-defaults" path="templates/linked-defaults" />
